articles.title: Burundi Food Security Outlook, October 2026 - May 2027: Low income, high prices drive Crisis in north; aid to refugees at risk amid funding shortage
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages FEWS NET estimates humanitarian food assistance needs will peak at 750,000–999,999 people during October and November, when Season B stocks are exhausted but Season A green harvests are not yet available. The populations of highest concern are refugees, returnees, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and poor households who have experienced consecutive seasons with large crop losses. Refugee camps in Burundi are expected to experience Stressed! (IPC Phase 2!) outcomes between October and January, with food assistance preventing worse outcomes. Cuts to food assistance for refugees are expected from January. The lack of own food production and high competition for limited labor opportunities, amid reduced humanitarian assistance, will drive Crisis (IPC Phase 3) between February-May. Should funding become accessible and assistance continues at the same or similar levels through May, Stressed! (IPC Phase 2!) outcomes would be expected to persist. The Northern Lowlands is expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) during the lean period of October to December 2026, before improving to Stressed (IPC Phase 2) from January through May. Delayed and below average Season A rainfall in September and October has exacerbated longstanding issues of below-average wages and labor opportunities at the same time food stocks are seasonally depleted. The Season A harvest in January and February is expected to restore capacity to meet minimum food needs, which will then be sustained by seasonal labor opportunities from March to May. However, below-average wages, lack of cross-border opportunities in Rwanda, and above-average food prices will constrain households’ ability to afford non-food essentials after food purchases. Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected in the Eastern Lowlands and Imbo Plains through May. Seasonal depletion of food stocks is combining with elevated food prices and local pressures (in the east, heightened market demand from refugees and returnees; in the west, fuel shortages and restricted cross-border opportunities in DRC). Season A harvests will generate modest improvement in food access by replenishing household stocks and driving lower market prices; however, below-average bean production and income amid above-average food prices will constrain recovery. The analysis in this report is based on information available as of October 31, 2026.
